speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I am very happy now to invite Mr David Hoe.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: He has been waiting to raise this Adjournment Motion, I believe, for nine times.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This goes to show that persistence does pay.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Before I start, I would like to record my appreciation to the participants of Curiosity Credits Dialogue, organised by South-West Young People's Action Party, at the same time, my Clementi residents during my Clementi community run and also my Meet-the-People Session volunteers.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They have helped to refine this idea that I am about to share today.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is important, because if we want to have our own definition of success, the first step, it is really a function of knowing our interest and what our strengths are like.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They made it clear that we already have many schemes supporting children and students from disadvantaged background.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I then kind of figure out that Curiosity Credits, because it cuts through many different life stages – preschool, primary school, secondary school and beyond – I must admit, it was not too obvious where does this nicely sit under?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Is it under the Ministry of Social and Family Development?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Is it under MOE, or is it a combination of agencies?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Well, at the same time, I am also happy to report that since my maiden speech, I have seen ground-up pilots suggest that this idea has promise.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Within a few months, that spark fanned into flame and she produced a drawing reflected in Figure 1, to express thanks to the donor.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Others have tried a course and decided not to continue.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: That, too, is useful, because discovery is not just about finding what one likes.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: It is also about finding what is not a good fit.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: But some decisions shape the directions of our lives.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: For many of our young Singaporeans, one of this decisions comes very early, that is at the age of 16.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: After they are done with "N" levels or "O" levels, our youths than have to decide: "Do I go to polytechnic?

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: A student enrols into an engineering course without realising how much mathematics or technical thinking it requires.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: But he simply have chosen a pathway that does not match his strengths, interests or learning style.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: What then happens is this – he enrols into the course; he struggles; he loses motivation; his grades suffer.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Perhaps he can still graduate from the Institute of Technical Education (ITE) or polytechnic, with mediocre results, about 2.0 or 2.5 of Grade Point Average (GPA) out of 4.0.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: At this point, he wants to switch out, switch to another course or progress to the next level, but with a GPA of 2.0 or 2.5, he may find that his options are narrowed.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: A higher Nitec student want to move to polytechnic, but his grades might not qualify because his GPA is not strong enough.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Even if his GPA was decent, he is not able to switch course that easily because of the earlier course that he has chosen.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Likewise, a polytechnic student who entered engineering, but later discovered that he wants to do another field, may find that his grades and course background do not support the switch.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Over time, this then contributes to underemployment or mismatch between what he or she studies, and what he or she eventually does at work.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: In my interactions with youths, I have asked them and they say, some tell me: "I chose this, because my friend chose this", "I chose this course because my grades could qualify for this", "I chose this because I was told that this was a safe course".

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: And a recent conversation reflects this harsh reality.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: I spoke with someone who is a chief executive officer of a private equity and venture capital investment firm.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: He shared with me how his 16-year-old nephew this year made his polytechnic course selection.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: His nephew was good at principles of accounts.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Therefore, at 15 years old, his very loving uncle decided to help him find an internship at an accountancy firm.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: His nephew realised that he really does not enjoy the nature of accounting even though he does well at principles of accounts and he decided that accountancy was not something he wanted to pursue.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: So, when his uncle asked him this year, "Nephew, what did you then decide?" The nephew replied, "I chose maritime business." His uncle was perturbed.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: He asked, "Why?" The nephew said, "My good friend chose maritime business.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Hence, I am going there." His uncle later realised that his good friend's family business was in the maritime sector so that choice made sense for his friend.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: But it did not necessarily make sense for his nephew.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Some of our young people have networks that can create opportunities for them to gain better clarity.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Second, not every 16-year-old would have this uncle, mentor or family contact who can help them to think through their choices.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: In fact, Singapore has built a fairly extensive ecosystem that helps students think about their future.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Students today have access to the MySkillsFuture portal and CourseFinder to explore education and career pathways.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: We have the Education and Career Guidance (ECG) curriculum in schools.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Students can consult their teachers and ECG counsellors.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: There are open houses by our polytechnics and Institutes of Technical Education (ITEs).

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: And our schools offer co-curricular activities (CCAs), Learning for Life experiences and, in some cases, internships, externships, job shadowing for some of our integrated programme schools.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: However, from the student's perspective, the exposure journey may still be uneven.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Some of this support I mentioned earlier, they are information-rich but lack hands-on.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: They can read about courses, but that is different from being able to try them.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Because our ECG counsellors can guide a student through, but it will be even better if they can reflect on something that is more concrete in their experience.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Some students may get internships or job shadowing or informal exposure before making such choices.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: But what I am asking is can we connect them more deliberately so that every student, especially those who come from less-resourced families, has a fair chance to taste and try before making a major post-secondary school decision.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Some may ask me, David, does it really matter?

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: It does if we fundamentally believe that every child learns differently.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: If we believe that some students learn better with hands-on experience, then it matters, because these hands-on experiences are not a nice-to-have.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: It helps them to make sense of their options.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: So, Mr Speaker, I would, therefore, like to ask whether MOE can study and pilot a more structured way to help students who learn best through experience.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: For now, let me call this Curiosity Credit 2.0.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: With this particular wallet, they can purchase curated taster sessions to have a flavour of what this course is like.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: These taster sessions are designed by ITEs, polytechnics, universities or specialised institutions, and schools can bring these tasters into the school and into the classrooms during selected weeks and also allow students to attend them at these institutions during protected exposure periods.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: The aim here is not to create an open-ended voucher scheme.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: This is why, in Figure 2, Curiosity Credits 2.0 is not just a passive wallet, it is a school-guided cycle.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Then, they enrol into one of these courses with guidance from their ECG counsellors or teachers.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Now, they experience a short and age-appropriate module.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: After that, they reflect on what they have learnt and then, use that, record it down, and decide on what the post-secondary choices will look like.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Follow me to Figure 3, because Figure 3 will show Members what it does look like across the secondary school years.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: More importantly, it is to reduce the possibility of underemployment.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Now that Members understand the broad strokes, let me bring Members through the details of how this work.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: What I am proposing is that these taster lessons, it should be age-appropriate.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: It should designed for secondary school students so that they can understand.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: One practical model is to expose them by broad cluster rather than an overwhelming list of courses.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: So, for example, this cluster could be health and care, engineering and the built environment, digital and cybersecurity, hospitality and tourism and the list goes on.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: A taster in engineering could show students not just the final exciting end-product, but to also show them the kind of mathematics, systems thinking and problem-solving required.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: What does a taster in nursing look like?

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: It could help them to understand the basics of patient care, empathy, clinical discipline and the realities of healthcare work.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: What does a taster in cybersecurity look like?

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: It could involve a simple hands-on challenge to show them what the field actually demands.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Exposure helps students to make more informed decisions.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Course design aside, let us move on to the mechanism.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: The mechanism and how it drives this exposure should be simple.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: First, as mentioned, each student will receive a certain number of credits to be able to purchase approved taster modules.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: The taster modules could be offered during maybe the last week of the school term or during protected exposure periods.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: By going for the taster lessons, it gives our teachers and our ECG counsellors something richer to discuss with the students.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: This can be linked to our ECG lessons because before the student goes for our taster lesson, the teacher can ask, "What course do you think you want to do?” After they have attended, instead of asking "What did you hope to do?", the question becomes, "What have you tried?

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: What made you want to learn more?" This, in my view, is a better ECG classroom conversation.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: It should be credits and entitlement used for approved programmes.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Second, it should be curated, not an open marketplace.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: The first set of providers could be from our ITE, polytechnics, universities or even specialised institutions.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Third, it should not be used for tuition, exam preparation or academic drilling.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Fourth, it should be easy for schools to administer.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: The Ministry can build upon the existing applied learning modules infrastructure.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: The question is not whether every taster leads to a course application.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Rather, the question should be – through every taster, does the student become clearer, more confident and more informed about their choices?

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: With the mechanism done, allow me to also say this: MOE already has something close to this.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: I see that as a strength to build upon, not as a reason to stop.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: What I have proposed and what I am proposing?

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: It tells the student – you have the permission to explore, and you have the choices to make.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Second, at the choice level, the tasters should cover a broad spread of clusters, like I mentioned earlier, health and care, engineering and the built environment, and the list goes on.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Because the current one today, is a multi-day module.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: While they have value, but shorter tasters will allow students to have a sample of more fields before narrowing down a choice.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: The goal is exposure and it is to spark.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Because if curiosity matters, we must create space for it.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: At the core, if we agree that every child learns differently, then the broad spectrum of intervention must be able to reflect that.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: At the heart of it, it is just like Curiosity Credits 1.0.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: This is fundamentally about helping each child to discover his or her interests.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Oftentimes, our ability to discover our interests depends on our access to opportunities.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: As we progress as a country, opportunity inequality exists.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Sometimes, well-meaning adults will tell students who do not know what to study and the easy advice is – just go to junior college first.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: For some of these students, this might work.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: If they are academically strong or if they prefer a more academic curriculum or want more time before specialising, junior college could be a good option.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: But it is not good advice for everyone.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: The student may or will struggle to obtain the grades needed for university and may emerge out with fewer options than expected.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: The issue is not whether junior college, polytechnic or ITE is better.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: This is why exposure matters before the choice is made.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: We often tell our youths that you must be able to define success for yourself.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: But in order to be able to define success for ourselves, we must first have some self-level of awareness.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: They must know what excites them, what challenges them, what kind of things they are willing to work hard for and what kind of environments will help them to grow.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Self-awareness does not magically happen at the age of 16.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: I want to build a Singapore where our youths are able to articulate their aspirations not because someone told them what to choose, but because they have discovered something about themselves in their own journey.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: If we truly believe in many different definitions of success, then we must allow our students to have the chance to see enough paths, enough possibilities and choose the next step with confidence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Experience is indeed a great teacher and we are open to ideas, like Mr Hoe's, that can bolster our existing range of programmes to guide our students in their educational journeys.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: But I would also like to gently offer a different perspective on one aspect of Mr Hoe's Motion – that is not having the perfect fit at 16 means it could be too late.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Certainly, not everyone must have everything figured out in secondary school to succeed in life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Members will already see some parallels with Mr Hoe's proposal.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: First, MOE offers exposure opportunities for our students at key junctures in their educational journey to understand how their choices today may shape their options tomorrow.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Within the school curriculum, MOE supports students in making informed education and career choices and prepares them for lifelong learning.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: In secondary school, students explore the diverse pathways available to them through ECG programmes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: This exploration allows them to develop a deeper understanding of their sense of purpose, their interests and their strengths.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Through education and career fairs and learning journeys, students are better equipped to make key decisions on subject combinations and post-secondary education pathways.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Institutes of higher learning (IHLs) offer flexible pathways to give students time and space to explore their interests and strengths.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: With the opportunity to be exposed to different areas and skill sets in their cluster for up to a year, students can make informed decisions about their specialisations, allaying to some extent Mr David Hoe's concern about the risk of course mismatch and its implications.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Beyond the curriculum, MOE provides students with opportunities to get a taste of the next stage of their schooling or working life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: As Mr David Hoe has pointed out, a hands-on approach will help students define success for themselves and explore areas that they may wish to grow into and aspire towards.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Our ECG Counsellors and Career Coaches stay current with emerging trends through professional development and networking sessions, to better provide our students with the personalised information and guidance to navigate the opportunities available for them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: In addition, polytechnics and ITE also conduct school visits and open houses, providing exposure to course offerings and an authentic taste of what student life could be like in these institutions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Second, MOE works with a network of community and industry partners to offer a wide range of authentic, real-world experiences in higher education and industry.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Our Partnerships Engagement Office actively reaches out to schools and industry organisations to identify and support partnerships that enrich learning for our students.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Our partners serve as mentors and role models, offering advice and internship opportunities that indeed expose students to diverse pathways.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: The Applied Learning Programme connects classroom learning with real-world applications, providing opportunities for students to appreciate the relevance and value of their learning beyond the classroom.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Partnerships with community and industry partners help students explore and develop their strengths and interests further in areas such as business and entrepreneurship, engineering and robotics, and journalism and broadcasting.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: For example, Peirce Secondary School has a partnership with Thales Singapore focused on exposing students to engineering and technology careers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: This year, students will experience an assembly career talk, visits and a work shadowing programme.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: This partnership supports students in fostering interest in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) fields through authentic industry learning experiences, to help make sense of their options as mentioned by Mr David Hoe.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Secondary schools also organise learning journeys to organisations and dialogues with community and industry partners.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: MOE welcomes more school-to-industry partnerships to open more opportunities for our students in our schools.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: In our polytechnics and ITE too, there are various efforts to help students transition from school to work, with the support of industry and community mentors.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: One example is the collaboration between Mentoring SG as well as the polytechnics and ITE, under which mentors work with polytechnic and ITE students to guide them on their longer-term career and life goals.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Daryl Thoe, a culinary student at Temasek Polytechnic and a young aspiring chef, went through Mentoring SG's programme last year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: His mentor, Irene Hamons, a private dining host and creative entrepreneur provided practical guidance on improving his culinary skills and coached him in goal setting.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: These helped him gain confidence and clarity on his goals that now drive his culinary aspirations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Third, MOE dedicates additional resources to support and empower students from disadvantaged backgrounds in their exploration of options and opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: These include our schools' wide range of co-curricular activities, as well as talent and enrichment programmes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: These workshops are complemented with job tasters or learning journeys to organisations across various industries.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Schools also work with other Government agencies and community partners like self-help groups, Social Service Offices (SSOs) and Family Service Centres (FSCs) to engage such students to develop their aspirations and broaden their perspectives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Under MSF's ComLink+ programme, dedicated SSO family coaches and FSC case workers work with lower-income families with children below 21, to support the child's education while helping the family address broader challenges that may affect their progress towards their long-term goals.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Many of us know from our own lives that the journey of learning and discovery rarely unfolds in a straight line.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: There are moments of clarity, but also moments of doubt, of redirection and most importantly, of growth.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Hock Yang initially wanted to follow in his brother's footsteps into Aerospace Engineering, but soon realised that it was not his cup of tea while pursuing a diploma in that field.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: After National Service, he reflected on his interests and took up a Diploma in Supply Chain Management at Republic Polytechnic.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: For his final year project, Hock Yang worked with his team to develop a solution to optimise air freight container space utilisation, a persistent challenge in logistics.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: He was awarded the LF Logistics Scholarship in 2024 and the prestigious Lee Foundation Scholarship in 2025.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Moving forward, Hock Yang now plans to pursue a degree in Infrastructure and Project Management at National University of Singapore, a far cry from his initial interest in Aerospace Engineering.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Hock Yang's story is just one of many.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Some might not take the most direct route to a work-ready qualification or may return as adult learners to upgrade to a diploma or degree at a later stage in life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: This is why we have worked hard to ensure that our education system remains responsive and walks alongside our students at all life stages, as their interests deepen and aspirations evolve.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: This can only be done with the support of family, community and industry partners.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi)
text: Let us continue to work together to support our children's curiosity and aspirations, and help them fulfil their potential, regardless of family background or starting point in life – for every child learns differently.
